title: Instructions in the Margin
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 5 of 40
content:
The book was wedged behind a row of cracked cauldrons and covered in enough dust to suggest that even Severus Snape had forgotten it existed.

I pulled it free and sneezed.

From the other side of the storeroom, Snape said, “If you contaminate the ingredients, I will have you removed.”

“With what authority?”

“Personal conviction.”

“Terrifying.”

I wiped the cover with my sleeve.

Advanced Potion-Making.

The title meant nothing unusual until I opened it.

Then I saw the handwriting.

Small. Dense. Slanting. Corrections packed into margins. Ingredients crossed out and replaced. Brewing times adjusted by minutes. Tiny observations threaded between printed instructions like a second, more intelligent book growing inside the first.

I stopped breathing for a moment.

Snape heard the silence.

“What?”

I held up the book.

He went still.

“Oh,” he said.

It was the least articulate thing I had heard from him.

I looked back at the page.

“Crush instead of cut.”

“Give me that.”

“Clockwise after every seventh counterclockwise turn.”

“Now.”

“You corrected the textbook.”

“It was wrong.”

“You were sixteen.”

“It remained wrong regardless of my age.”

He crossed the room faster than he should have and took the book from my hands.

His face had shut down, but not before I saw embarrassment.

Actual embarrassment.

It was astonishing.

“You're blushing,” I said.

“I am not.”

“You are.”

“My circulation is affected by medication.”

“Of course.”

“Do you wish to continue working here?”

“Desperately.”

He tucked the book under his arm.

I should have let it go.

Instead I said, “That is brilliant work.”

Snape stopped.

The silence changed.

I had praised him before, lightly, usually to irritate him. This was different. I meant it without humor.

He did not turn around.

“The printed instructions wasted sopophorous juice,” he said.

“That doesn't make the correction less brilliant.”

“It is an adjustment.”

“It's an adjustment a published author failed to find.”

“Published authors fail to find many things.”

“That sounded personal.”

“Most truths do.”

He placed the book on a high shelf behind his desk.

I returned to the cauldrons.

Ten minutes later, he brought it back.

He set it beside my hand.

“You may examine it,” he said.

I looked up.

“Under supervision.”

“Naturally.”

“And you will not remove it from this room.”

“I wouldn't.”

“And you will not speak of the contents to Potter.”

I blinked.

“Harry Potter?”

Snape's expression sharpened.

“How many Potters do you imagine I mean?”

“I don't know. You're very committed to grudges. There could be a list.”

His mouth twitched.

“Why would I speak to him about it?”

“Because he used it.”

I stared at the book.

Then at Snape.

“The Boy Who Lived learned Potions from your school notes?”

“Do not phrase it like that.”

“How should I phrase it?”

“He stole my textbook.”

“Was your name in it?”

“No.”

“Then technically—”

“Do not.”

I laughed.

The book turned out to be more revealing than any confession Snape might have offered.

Not because it contained secrets about his life. It did not. It contained impatience.

Young Snape had hated inefficiency.

He had questioned every instruction. Tested every assumption. Refused to respect authority that could not survive evidence. He had written insults in the margins beside clumsy methods, sometimes only a single question mark sharp enough to function as contempt.

There were spells too.

Some harmless.

Some clever.

Some not.

I paused over one marked for enemies.

Snape saw where my eyes had stopped.

His face went very quiet.

“Later,” he said.

Not never.

Later.

I closed the book.

“Agreed.”

He seemed surprised.

I returned to the safer pages.

A note beside a burn-healing paste recommended adding powdered silver last instead of first. I frowned.

“That would reduce scarring.”

“Yes.”

“Why isn't this standard practice?”

“Because healers repeat what they are taught.”

“So do potioneers.”

“Bad ones.”

I looked at the pale marks on his throat.

“Did you use it?”

His hand rose unconsciously to his collar.

“Not initially.”

“Because you were unconscious.”

“Yes.”

“Pomfrey?”

“Eventually.”

“Did it help?”

“A little.”

The answer was softer than I expected.

I turned another page.

The margins became more crowded in later chapters, as though the boy writing them had grown bolder. There were entire replacement methods squeezed between lines.

“What did your professor think?” I asked.

“That I was insufferable.”

“Accurate.”

“Indeed.”

“And talented?”

He did not answer.

I looked up.

Snape was watching the book, not me.

“No one said it?”

“That is an absurd question.”

“Is it?”

“Yes.”

I waited.

He turned away.

That was answer enough.

Something in me ached unexpectedly.

Not pity. I had promised myself not to reduce him to a collection of wounds. But there was something bleak about imagining a boy filling margins with discoveries and learning that brilliance could be ignored if the person carrying it was difficult enough to dislike.

Then again, Snape had likely made himself very easy to dislike.

Both things could be true.

I tapped the page.

“This should be published.”

He looked at me as if I had suggested public nudity.

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I said so.”

“That is not a reason. That's a classroom shortcut.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You think I don't recognize the difference?”

“I think you use authority when explanation would cost more.”

He became very still.

I had done it again: stepped too close to whatever he kept behind the doors.

But this time he did not reach for his wand.

He sat down.

“The notes are mine,” he said. “Some were written by a child who believed cleverness was sufficient protection. Some by an adolescent who mistook cruelty for strength. Some are useful. Some are dangerous. I have no desire to package that mixture for strangers to admire.”

I considered him.

“That is a reason.”

“Yes.”

“I still think the useful parts deserve daylight.”

“They have survived thirty years without it.”

“So have you.”

His eyes snapped to mine.

The sentence hung between us.

I had not planned it.

Neither of us seemed to know what to do with it.

At last Snape said, “A regrettable comparison.”

“Maybe.”

I turned back to the book.

He let me keep reading.

Near the back, I found a potion I did not recognize. There was no printed recipe, only his handwriting across a blank page.

The ingredients formed a protective tonic: dittany, asphodel, bezoar extract, a carefully measured venom neutralizer, and a stabilizing agent usually used in long-duration brews.

My pulse quickened.

“This is the antivenom.”

He said nothing.

“The one you were taking before the battle.”

Still nothing.

I read the notes.

DOSAGE: 7 DAYS MINIMUM FOR TISSUE SATURATION.

LIMITED EFFICACY AGAINST UNKNOWN SERPENT VENOMS.

DO NOT RELY ON AS SOLE TREATMENT.

BLOOD-LOSS RISK UNAFFECTED.

I looked at him.

“You knew.”

“I suspected.”

“That Nagini might be used against you.”

“I had observed her diet.”

The dry delivery made the horror worse.

“You prepared for your own murder.”

“I prepared for a range of foreseeable outcomes.”

“That's a very Snape way to say it.”

“An astonishing observation, given that I am Snape.”

I traced the edge of the page without touching the ink.

“You wrote not to rely on it as sole treatment.”

“Yes.”

“But you went anyway.”

His eyes hardened.

“There was nowhere else to go.”

“That isn't true.”

“It was at the time.”

I wanted to argue.

Instead I looked at the formula.

A potion designed by a man who expected death and still made one last technical correction against it.

“You saved yourself,” I said.

Snape's expression turned strange.

“No.”

“The potion kept you alive long enough to be found.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It is from where I'm standing.”

He closed the book.

“Then stand somewhere else.”

The words were sharp, but his voice broke slightly on the last one.

Pain.

Throat, memory, or both.

I did not push.

We spent the rest of the afternoon cataloguing cauldrons.

Just before dinner, he placed the textbook in my hands.

“Take it,” he said.

I stared at him.

“To your quarters. You wished to examine the useful sections.”

“What about your rule?”

“I am revising it.”

“Why?”

His expression became familiar sarcasm again, a coat he could put on quickly.

“Because watching you read is intolerably distracting.”

I held the book against my chest.

“I'll bring it back tomorrow.”

“You will bring it back tonight if there is so much as a bent corner.”

“Yes, Professor.”

His eyes flashed.

I smiled.

He looked away first.

That evening, I read the margins until after midnight.

Not because I wanted to solve Severus Snape.

I was beginning to understand that he was not a puzzle placed in front of me for entertainment.

I read because the mind in those pages was fierce, impatient, inventive, wounded, arrogant, and alive.

And because, for reasons I was not yet willing to name, he had trusted me with it.
